newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia's Telstra welcomes sale approval.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia's Telstra welcomes sale approval.

text.p: Australian government-owned telecommunicataions carrier Telstra Corp said on Thursday it welcomed the Australian Senate's appoval of the one-third sale the company, which is expected to occur in early 1998.

"This historic step will significantly improve Australia's ability to reap the benefits of the telecommunications revolution that is now happening around the world," Telstra chief executive officer Frank Blount said in a statement.
"Partial privatisation of Telstra will bring clear benefits, particularly in terms of exposure to market disciplines and scrutiny and a stronger commercial focus," Blount said.

"Competition is, and will continue to be, the primary driving force for Telstra. But partial privatisation will allow the company and its staff to magnify the benefits deriving from that competition," Blount said.
Blount said that the programs Telstra had committed to in Tasmania and Queensland met the company's broad national planning parameter.

All non-government parties opposed the sale bill, which passed the upper house by a bare margin with the support of two independents, one each from Tasmania and Queensland, who the government had wooed with promises of money for the home states.

"We are undergoing major change, including a significant reduction in Telstra employment over the next three years. But the company remains committed to improving service and providing all Australians with the most modern communications infrastructure," Blount said.
The sale of Telstra is the largest in a long line of privatisations that has seen such Australian assets as Qantas Airways Ltd and the Commonwealth Bank of Australia pass into private hands.
The government has been assuming that the sale will raise A$8 billion, but analysts said the stake would probably be worth closer to A$12 billion.
International investors can take a one third stake in the privatisation, with each individual foreign investor limited to five percent.
